analysis.one_liner: Creates a Medicare-run prescription drug plan with government-negotiated drug prices and a $35 monthly premium.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on March 30, 2004 and never received a vote, dying when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed the new Medicare Part D drug benefit so that, alongside private drug plans, the government itself would offer a Medicare-operated drug plan available nationwide. The plan would have negotiated drug prices directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers and charged a uniform premium of $35 a month in 2006. The 2003 Medicare law had barred the government from negotiating prices and left the drug benefit entirely to private insurers, so this bill was a direct challenge to that structure.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, roughly the tens of millions of seniors and people with disabilities who would qualify for the new Part D benefit. They would gain a guaranteed government-run plan available everywhere in the country, with a known $35 monthly premium in 2006 and drug prices negotiated by the government rather than set by private plan contracts with manufacturers.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to offer one or more Medicare-operated prescription drug plans nationwide, in addition to private plans, beginning in 2006.

Requires the Secretary to negotiate with pharmaceutical manufacturers to reduce the purchase cost of covered Part D drugs and to encourage use of more affordable therapeutic equivalents where medically appropriate.
Sets the plan's beneficiary premium at $35 a month for 2006, uniform nationwide, with at least one plan guaranteed at that price, and allows supplemental coverage at an adjusted premium.
Allows the Secretary to designate the Medicare-operated plan as a fallback plan in areas where private plans are inadequate, so beneficiaries in underserved areas would have an option.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would face a buyer negotiating prices down on Medicare's enormous drug volume, and private drug plan insurers, who would compete against a government-run plan. Taxpayers could also bear part of the cost if the actuarial cost of the public plan exceeded the $35 premium.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers and private drug plan insurers

drawbacks.text: Negotiating prices down and steering patients to cheaper therapeutic equivalents would cut manufacturer revenue, which critics warned could reduce the returns that fund pharmaceutical research and development; the bill guards medical necessity but does not address the innovation argument.

A nationwide $35 premium keyed to average per capita cost could diverge from actual costs in high-cost regions or as drug prices changed, creating a gap that would have to be covered by federal subsidies.

A government-run plan competing with private drug plans could draw enrollment away from those private plans, and the bill lets the Secretary designate the public plan as the fallback in areas, expanding the government's role beyond what the 2003 Medicare law contemplated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For beneficiaries the potential gain is straightforward: a government plan that negotiates prices the way other large federal purchasers do, at a fixed $35 premium. The main costs fall on drug manufacturers and private insurers rather than on beneficiaries, though taxpayers could absorb premium shortfalls. The bill is a fairly clean instrument for its purpose, but it died without the committee ever weighing those trade-offs publicly.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it sat there until the Congress ended without any vote.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on March 30, 2004, with Senators Dayton and Levin; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action appears in the record: no hearings, no markups, no committee report, and no floor vote before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

The bill targeted the structure created by the 2003 Medicare drug law, which prohibited the government from negotiating drug prices under Part D and relied entirely on private plans, so enacting it would have rewritten a benefit that had just been enacted the year before.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and private Medicare drug plan insurers kept the Part D structure intact: no government negotiation of drug prices and no public plan competing with them. Seniors gained nothing from the bill's proposed negotiated-price option.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and private drug plan insurers

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 30, 2004 to create a Medicare-operated drug plan with negotiated prices.

for.name: Sen. Mark Dayton
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as an original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup, reported the bill out, or scheduled any action after referral; the bill died in committee when the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Had passed the 2003 Medicare drug law barring price negotiation and took up no legislation to revisit it; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored this bill.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsorship and cosponsorship was Democratic (three senators), with no Republican support in the record, in a Congress where Republicans controlled the Senate and had just passed the 2003 drug law this bill sought to amend.

industries.note: The bill would have required the government to negotiate purchase prices for Part D drugs and push cheaper therapeutic equivalents, cutting into manufacturers' pricing power on Medicare's huge drug volume. The 2003 law had specifically barred such negotiation, keeping the industry's pricing position protected.

Part D was built to route the drug benefit entirely through private plans; this bill would have added a competing government-run plan available nationwide with a fixed $35 premium. Private plans would keep operating but would face a public competitor that could also be designated as the fallback in underserved areas.
